script: My moderator boss tried to expose bots—now I am caught in their revenge plot.. I was scrolling through r/MaliciousCompliance, and the mod team dropped a note that felt like a textbook on why we're all here. They said, "Fictional stories aren't new to this community, and Rule 3 exists because of that." (I know, right?) I mean, who even knows what Rule 3 actually says? It's like, "Some stories of well‑written fiction will get posted, some stories of terribly written truth will get posted." The audacity of it—like, do we even care if it's fiction or not? Not when bots are out here building fake histories just to spam us later. The first line hit me like a punch: "Bot accounts posting generative content are not here to share a story." That's the real kicker. They're not sharing. They're building a realistic‑looking thread to sneak in product promos. And you, my bestie, you're probably thinking, "Okay, fine, I'll ignore it." But the mod team was straight up saying: Don't comment on suspicious posts. Don't even say "this looks fake" or "Laughing out loud this is AI." Every comment, no matter how dumb, just gives the bot more reach. Rule 3 is absolute—no exceptions. (Literally insane.) So what do you do? They're telling us to report instead. Report under Manipulated Content or Spam, or hit Rule 4: "Follow Original Content Policy." Reporting is the only reliable way to get those shady threads taken down. They admit some posts slip through, and reviews can take a minute, but that's the best tool we've got. In the end, the mod team's note was just a reminder: we're not here to play detective with our comments. We're here to keep the subreddit clean. So next time you see a post that feels off, don't comment. Just hit that report button. Trust me, you'll thank yourself later.
